title: New Housing Fund Rules: Take What You Can, But Don't Treat It as Savings
dek: The housing provident fund is not savings you can withdraw at will — fraudulent withdrawal gets you pursued for repayment and barred from any withdrawal for three years. But the new rules put renting first in the withdrawal order and scrap the rent-to-income ratio cap, so money you should take, you should still take.
why: Three people in different situations — a self-employed worker, a young professional, and a property owner — each run their own numbers, turning the new rules' 20 clause changes into concrete decisions. The second half, on flexible-employment contributions and the contrast with the system-inside track, is especially informative.
who: Employees with a housing fund who aren't sure whether to withdraw or leave it; people considering buying a home, converting a commercial loan to a provident-fund loan, or contributing as flexible-employment workers; job seekers trying to judge whether a company is well-run.
skip: The opening chat about how the episode came about and where the three hosts stand can be fast-forwarded; start at 13:10, where Zhou Yi's experience of using it begins.

points.h: Six months after auto-withdrawal, I paused it myself
points.body: After Zhou Yi turned on Beijing's no-threshold monthly rent withdrawal of 2,000 yuan, she found the money slid into another card the moment it arrived, completely decoupled from the mental account for paying rent; when her spending card ran out at month's end, the money was auto-deducted, which only added friction to life. Once she confirmed the fund balance earns 1.5% interest — above the roughly 0.95% on a one-year bank time deposit — she paused the withdrawal the next day. Yubai notes this contrasts with the advice three years ago to ‘take everything you can, use everything you can’, and two young colleagues in the department have made the same choice. Lao Qian cautions that this is indeed a low-efficiency use of funds, but most people can't achieve the efficiency they imagine for themselves — people just keep fake books for themselves.

points.h: The housing fund is not savings; not being able to withdraw is the norm
points.body: Yubai walks through an extreme case: a young person loses their job and goes home with no liquid funds, tens of thousands of yuan sitting in the housing fund, but the home is self-occupied, so it qualifies neither as buying nor as renting; even if the new rules allow withdrawal under the names of renovation or property fees, if the family has no such needs, there is nothing to be done. If you risk it and invent a pretext for fraudulent withdrawal, you will be pursued to return the entire amount and barred from withdrawing any housing fund for three years. So both approaches hold — ‘take everything you can’ and ‘treat it as forced savings at a rate above demand deposits’ — and the key is the individual's situation.

points.h: The new rules put renting first in the withdrawal order
points.body: This revision adjusts 20 clauses in total. First, renovating a self-occupied home and paying property fees on a self-occupied home are included as withdrawal purposes for the first time; the fund no longer serves only loan-financed home purchases. Second, renting withdrawal used to require that rent exceed a set proportion of household wage income; this version removes that restriction, and renting is placed first in the withdrawal order. Third, flexible-employment workers are formally brought into the system for the first time: self-employed individuals and part-time workers may contribute voluntarily and apply for provident-fund loans. In addition, the management center should reply to withdrawal applications within three days and to loan applications within ten days, and nationwide mutual recognition of contribution records is being pushed forward.

points.h: The share of contributions lent out has fallen from 70% to 30%
points.body: The figure Lao Qian saw: this year, the share of housing fund contributions lent out is as low as just over 30%, versus over 70% at the peak — a steady decline in just a few years. In other words, the theoretically most stable, lowest-rate, highest-quality lending channel is actually used by only a bit over 30% of people. That directly reflects how low the willingness to buy is. Lao Qian also points out that the new rules point toward housing consumption rather than leverage: renting moved to first place, property fees and renovation can be withdrawn, thresholds cut sharply — supporting measures as the property market shifts from an incremental to a stock phase, and also echoing the aging trend: the monthly withdrawal ratio turned up in 2023, exactly matching the retirement of the 1960s cohort.

points.h: If you want to buy, be careful about withdrawing your housing fund
points.body: Yubai warns: provident-fund loan limits are tied to account balance — in some cities you can borrow 16 times the balance, in others 20 times, varying by city. Guangzhou also has multiple caps, and at application the smallest of several standards applies: for a first or second self-occupied home the minimum down payment is 20%, so on a 1 million yuan home the loan cannot exceed 800,000; and a monthly repayment exceeding 50% of monthly income also fails. So before withdrawing your housing fund as living expenses, check your city's loan rules. Yubai is also cautious about the buy-side logic that ‘the rental yield is close to the provident-fund rate, and only the down payment is missing’: you still have to weigh depreciation, price swings, and how to withstand risk once a 600,000 yuan down payment is locked up.

points.h: Flexible-employment contributors carry the full amount alone
points.body: For flexible-employment workers the contribution base and ratio are calculated the same way as for employees, but no employer pays half, so one person bears the full 10% to 24%. The base must be self-declared: below 10,000 yuan no proof is needed; above 10,000 you must log into the individual income tax app and pull your tax details as documentation, to prevent inflating the base to extract a higher loan limit. Zhou Yi ran the numbers: on 10,000 yuan, 10% to 24% is 1,000 to 2,400 yuan, and this money is not counted in individual income tax, but it is a loss if you never use it. In addition, most pilot cities require 6 to 12 consecutive months of contributions before you can apply for a provident-fund loan, and most do not allow one-off back payments.

points.h: Inside the system, the housing fund is an invisible benefit
points.body: Zhou Yi asked a friend back home with a public-institution post, who readily showed a screenshot of her housing fund account: the monthly deposit is more than twice Zhou Yi's, and the balance already exceeds her savings. The friend lives at home with no rental need, so the fund just accumulates as forced savings or future loan capacity, and she also has an occupational annuity, with the contribution base counting bonuses and subsidies in full. Lao Qian adds: the housing fund is tax-free, and on top of that private pensions cap contributions at 12,000 yuan a year and tax 3% on withdrawal, so being inside the system already carries an extra layer of tax advantage. On the data: in 2025 the average annual wage of urban non-private unit employees nationwide was 129,441 yuan, versus 71,590 yuan for private units — while working hours run the other way.

points.h: Full housing fund contributions are a slice for judging a company
points.body: Lao Qian's judgment on whether ‘a company that pays the housing fund is a more desirable choice’ has not changed at all: a company that pays the housing fund in full shows it respects employees and respects the rules, which means it is probably well-run in every respect, and won't play cat-and-mouse with policy. He goes further: this points to not making profit maximization the first goal, to treating people as people, and the invisible returns show up elsewhere. Zhou Yi has run the numbers: on a wage base of 100, take-home is just over 70, but the boss pays out over 130, and everyone along the chain feels aggrieved. Lao Qian cites Ford's Model T wage increase — letting workers afford a car and have time to use it wasn't capitalist conscience, it was simply a better utility function.

quotes.text: It arrived, but because your phone gets so many app notifications you don't look carefully — say it reminds you 2,000 yuan came in, and then it just sits in that card until the end of the month, when my spending card is used up and it gets auto-deducted from that card.
But the fact is people keep fake books for themselves, people withdraw on impulse for all sorts of reasons, people are very good at self-deception.
You really can't treat the housing fund as a deposit, because your bank deposit you can withdraw at any time, but the housing fund you can't.
And it's the highest-quality lending channel, the rate is so low, yet only a bit over 30% of people took out loans — and at the peak, what was that share? Over 70%. In just a few years.
I think a company that pays the housing fund in full shows it respects employees and respects the rules.

Treating people as people doesn't mean raising costs — it also means one person's spending, the household sector's spending, becomes the corporate sector's income, and the corporate sector's spending becomes the household sector's wages. Those two are a virtuous cycle.
Take everything you can, use everything you can — buying a home, building, renovating, repaying a loan, renting, retirement, leaving the country — all of it can be used.
